edits.old: A rebuild after a drop is a new createIndex operation on the current collection data, not an immediate reversal of dropIndexes. MongoDB documents that index builds on populated collections hold an exclusive collection lock briefly at the start and end, while yielding to reads and writes during the rest of the build; this build-lock behavior differs from dropIndexes holding its lock for the full removal operation. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-23)

edits.rationale: The index-creation page says builds hold an exclusive lock briefly at the beginning and end and yield to reads and writes for the rest. The dropIndex page says the drop holds an exclusive collection lock for the whole operation. A rebuild is a fresh createIndex build, which is the plain meaning of the two pages together.

edits.old: dropIndexes kills queries that use the index being removed, including queries still considering it during planning. After the drop, the planner cannot use that index; reads can regress if the remaining plan is slower, so validate critical query shapes and representative traffic before and after removal. (medium confidence)
edits.new: dropIndexes only kills queries that are using the index being dropped, which may include queries considering the index as part of query planning. After the drop, the planner cannot use that index; the optimizer may choose a different existing index, so verify critical query shapes with explain() before and after removal. Sources: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/v8.0/reference/command/dropindexes/ ; https://www.netdata.cloud/guides/mongodb/mongodb-unused-indexes/

edits.old: The MongoDB 7.0 and 8.0 command manuals describe the same dropIndexes locking behavior: it holds an exclusive lock on the target collection for the command's duration, and subsequent operations on that collection wait for release. The manuals do not describe this as an 8.0 change or as a database-wide lock; an independent operations guide dates the move from database to collection lock scope to MongoDB 4.2. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-23)

edits.old: Dropping an unused index can reduce write and storage overhead, but removing an index used by read queries can change plans and cause slower scans. Netdata advises dropping during lower traffic and monitoring lock waits and query plans afterward; Percona describes the read benefit and write and storage costs of indexes, supporting workload-specific validation rather than treating every unused-index result as safe for removal. (medium confidence)
